l: adversary-hammer prior, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: The adversary-hammer prior is a discrete, extreme reliability prior for worst-case evaluation and reliability-estimation distortion. It assigns low reliability to adversaries and higher reliability to a hammer, with four adversaries and one hammer. Its results appear in Table A4 and, with Llama2-7B, assess accuracy as adversaries increase from one to seven across Natural Questions, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA.

l: Oracle WMV, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Oracle WMV is a method and performance reference for accuracy and filtering comparisons. It assumes perfect knowledge of source reliability and uses reliability values as aggregation weights. In the reliability-estimation ablation it reaches 0.541 accuracy, providing an optimal oracle benchmark; RA-RAG is reported as comparable while relying on fewer sources.

l: Vanilla RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Vanilla RAG is a retrieval-augmented generation method and accuracy-comparison baseline. It retrieves top-10 documents without additional modules, takes 0.32 seconds per task, and is evaluated under adversary-hammer and beta priors. Its accuracy generally, and severely, declines as adversarial sources increase.

l: Robust RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Robust RAG is a certifiably robust defense framework and accuracy-comparison-baseline method for retrieval-augmented generation. It aggregates keywords from independent passages assuming most documents are trustworthy, but struggles with varying reliability and degrades as adversaries increase.

l: Self-RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Self-RAG is an advanced retrieval-augmented generation method, fine-tuned on Llama2-7B and included for fair comparison, evaluated on Natural Questions, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA with 7.44-second inference.

l: Vanilla LLM, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: is_a method [accuracy comparison baseline] It provides a non-retrieval comparison whose reported accuracy remains constant across adversary counts for each dataset and model.

l: Llama3-8B-Instruct, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Llama3-8B-Instruct is a language model used to evaluate RA-RAG. It supports main NQ and TQA comparisons, adversary-hammer and beta-prior reliability evaluations, κ and filtering ablations, and comparisons with and without κ-RRSS. Its accuracy is evaluated on NQ, TQA, and HotpotQA across multiple falign filtering thresholds.

l: Phi3-mini-Instruct, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: It is evaluated in the beta-prior experiments across different numbers of sources. Phi3-mini-Instruct is evaluated on NQ, TQA, and HotpotQA across multiple falign filtering thresholds.

l: GPT-4o-mini, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: GPT-4o-mini is a language model used in experiments and fact-checking setups. It paraphrases factual documents into nine versions per query and generates nine distinct incorrect answers with three misinformation documents for each. Although used to generate plausible misinformation, it often resists doing so and may reinsert correct answers, requiring careful prompts and manual post-processing. It is evaluated in beta-prior, NQ, TQA, and HotpotQA experiments, including RA-RAG and κ-RRSS accuracy and efficiency analyses.

l: Llama2-7B, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Llama2-7B is the model used in reported beta-prior and adversary-hammer experiments, evaluating accuracy on NQ, TQA, and HotpotQA, including Table A3.

l: Accuracy, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Accuracy is an evaluation metric for answer correctness, measured by whether a gold answer appears in a generated response and averaged over ten random trials. It is reported across datasets, methods, models, adversaries, sources, and prior settings. RA-RAG generally outperforms baselines and remains robust as adversaries increase; reported values include 0.947, 0.943, 0.801, 0.541, 0.537, and 0.490.

l: wall-clock time, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Wall-clock time is measured for inference per task and for reliability estimation across different numbers of sources. Inference takes 1.21 seconds with 5 sources and 1.82 seconds with 1,000 sources, while reliability estimation takes 4.65 minutes and 14.81 hours, respectively.

l: PolitiFact, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: PolitiFact is a fact-checking platform that collects claims, evaluates their truthfulness, and assigns verdict-based truthfulness labels.

l: Politician A, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Politician A is a prominent public figure evaluated in augmented real-world reliability estimation. Across 388 claims, 64 are true and 324 false; the method estimates reliability at 0.175 versus oracle 0.165, achieving 0.949 accuracy.

l: Politician B, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Politician B, a prominent public figure, is evaluated in augmented reliability-estimation experiments. Across 104 claims, 63 are true and 41 false; estimated reliability is 0.539 versus oracle 0.606, with 0.932 accuracy.

l: User A, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: User A is an X account sharing breaking news. Across January 1–13, 2025, it contributed 244 posts: 180 true and 64 false. In reliability-estimation experiments under augmented variation, its estimated reliability was 0.660 versus an oracle 0.738, with 0.795 accuracy; augmented results reached PCC 0.991, SRCC 0.992, and average accuracy 0.801.

l: Google News, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Google News is a retriever that supplies the top 20 relevant documents for a fact-checking process.

l: claims, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: The claims are collected from PolitiFact for Politician A and Politician B, with their truthfulness determined by PolitiFact's verdicts. The study evaluates the accuracy of responses to fact-checking queries about these claims.

l: posts (User A), Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: are_manually_verified_by fact-checking sites [by cross-checking] Posts from User A are collected from January 1–13, 2025, and manually verified by cross-checking with fact-checking sites. The collection contains 244 posts, of which 180 are true and 64 are false.

l: oracle reliability, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: has_range 0.1 to 0.9 [true-to-false ratio in augmented data] Oracle reliability is used as the reference for evaluating estimated reliability. The dataset is augmented by random sampling to vary the true-to-false ratio and produce oracle reliability levels from 0.1 to 0.9.

l: estimated reliability, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Estimated reliability closely aligns with oracle reliability for Politician A, Politician B, and User A. For User A, the estimates maintain strong linear and monotonic relationships with oracle reliability across augmented reliability levels.

l: Pearson Correlation Coefficient, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: It measures linear correlation between estimated and oracle reliability, yielding 0.998 for Politician A, 0.999 for Politician B, and 0.991 for User A under augmented variation, all p < 0.001.

l: Spearman Rank Correlation Coefficient, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Spearman Rank Correlation Coefficient measures monotonic relationships between estimated and oracle reliability, reporting 1.000 for Politician A and 0.992 for User A under augmented variation, both with p < 0.001.

l: short-form question answering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: The work focuses on short-form question answering, where RA-RAG is proposed to obtain reliable answers by accounting for source reliability during retrieval and generation.

l: multi-hop question answering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: RA-RAG is described as extending to multi-hop question answering. An LLM can decompose a task into atomic subquestions, apply the framework to obtain reliable answers, and then aggregate those answers.

l: datasets, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: comprise diverse sources [with heterogeneous reliability] The paper identifies the construction of datasets with diverse sources and heterogeneous reliability as a promising direction for more rigorous evaluation and the development of stronger source-aware methods.

l: long-form and multi-hop question answering datasets, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: A paper proposes diverse-source, heterogeneous-reliability long-form and multi-hop question answering datasets for rigorous evaluation and source-aware methods.

l: news-related claims, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: have abundant fact-checking sources [for cross-verification] News-related claims are a setting in which the reliability estimation method is particularly effective because abundant fact-checking sources are available.

l: specialized topics, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: present_application_challenges limited references for cross-verification Specialized topics are challenging for the reliability estimation method because they have limited references for cross-verification.

l: expert knowledge, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Expert knowledge is proposed as a promising alternative for cross-verification, potentially addressing reliability-estimation difficulties in specialized topics.

l: offline setting, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: requires periodic updates [to capture changes in source reliability over time] The framework operates in an offline setting, so it requires periodic updates to capture changes in source reliability over time.

l: periodic updates, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: can_be_performed efficiently [as demonstrated in Appendix J.2] Periodic updates are required to capture changes in source reliability over time. They can be performed efficiently, as demonstrated in Appendix J.2.

l: unreliable information, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Unreliable information may be disseminated in large volumes by sources that were previously considered reliable.

l: account hacking, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: can_cause reliable sources disseminating unreliable information [in cases of account hacking] Account hacking is given as an example of a situation in which a reliable source may suddenly disseminate large volumes of unreliable information.

l: online framework, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: An online framework is proposed for more responsive systems, continuously updating reliability estimates in real time to enable adaptive responses to evolving information.

l: evolving information landscape, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: receives adaptive responses [from an online framework] The evolving information landscape motivates the development of an online framework capable of continuously updating reliability estimates and responding adaptively in real time.

s: Misalignment filtration converts outputs into declarative sentences, evaluates alignment with relevant context using Alignscore, retains sufficiently scored outputs, replaces others with IDK, and studies the threshold.

s: Factual consistency evaluation assesses how well generated text aligns with the given context. AlignScore is used as the factual consistency evaluation method in this unit.

s: are_not declarative sentences [often] LLM outputs are often not declarative sentences, which makes direct consistency evaluation challenging. They are converted into declarative forms before being evaluated.

s: A sequence-to-sequence model attributed to Song (2022), previously used by Zha et al. (2023), converts outputs into declarative sentences, yielding ˆy∗i.

s: are_the_form_of LLM outputs [converted form] Declarative sentences are used as the converted form of outputs for consistency evaluation. Their use addresses the difficulty of evaluating LLM outputs that are not originally declarative.

s: is_embedded_in query [sometimes; important information] Context is what generated text is assessed against by AlignScore. Important contextual information can sometimes be embedded in the query, which makes direct consistency evaluation challenging.

s: evaluates declarative sentences [after conversion] The Alignscore function evaluates the declarative output ˆy∗i against R(q, Si). In the filtration rule, its score determines whether ˆyi is replaced with IDK or retained.

l: τ filtering threshold, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: τ is the misalignment filtering threshold. It is set to 0.1 in all experiments, following Lei et al. (2023), which identifies 0.1 as optimal for CNN and Daily Mail articles. Ablations compare 0.1, 0.5, and 0.8 with no filtering: higher values filter more misaligned responses but lose more aligned information.

l: reliability score, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Reliability scores determine the descending order in which sources are processed by κ-RRSS.

l: answers, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Answers are language-model outputs retained as non-IDK after falign or excluded when falign returns IDK. They are categorized as correct, incorrect, IDK, or hallucinated, with distributions reported by retrieved-document type and filtering threshold.

l: factual documents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Wikipedia material is retrieved using Contriever, paraphrased by GPT-4o-mini into nine equivalent documents per query, and filtering corresponds to lower Llama3-8B-Instruct accuracy.

l: misinformation documents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Misinformation documents, generated in groups of three for each of nine incorrect answers per query from designated sources, cause frequent misaligned LLM responses without falign. In a filtering ablation, filtering lowers correct answers from 5.05% to 2.53% and incorrect answers from 75.76% to 70.96%, while increasing IDK responses and reducing hallucinations.

l: irrelevant documents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: For irrelevant documents in a TQA filtering ablation on Llama3-8B-Instruct, filtering lowers correct answers from 26.07% to 4.16% and hallucinations from 22.89% to 4.53%, while raising IDK from 50.92% to 91.19%, replacing ungrounded responses with uncertainty.

l: correct answer, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: is_less_frequent_than incorrect answers [in the example described] The correct answer can appear less frequently than incorrect answers, yet RA-RAG can still estimate it accurately by assigning higher weights to more reliable sources.

l: incorrect answers, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Incorrect answers can appear more frequently than the correct answer in cases where RA-RAG still accurately estimates the correct answer.

l: hallucination, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Hallucination rates decrease with filtering, especially for irrelevant documents, while misinformation drops from 10.10% to 8.33%.

l: Ours with filtering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: Ours with filtering achieves accuracy 0.537 in the reliability-estimation ablation, where it is compared with Ours without filtering.

s: Filtering ablation study compares falign’s answer-type distributions across factual, misinformation, and irrelevant documents, evaluating accuracy on Llama3-8B-Instruct and TQA.

l: falign filtering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability
s: falign filtering is a filtering method evaluated across factual, misinformation, and irrelevant retrieved documents; varying its threshold reduces misaligned responses by replacing them with IDK and mitigates reliability-estimation weight distortion.

s: It is modeled by independently assigning sources different relevance and truthfulness properties, and is also evaluated using beta priors.

s: Its corpus is used to retrieve documents containing correct answers for Natural Questions, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA queries through Contriever.

s: Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA are used to generate the benchmark, with 1,600 queries selected from each dataset.

s: Figure A8 is a figure illustrating the instruction prompt used for answer generation.

s: is_evaluated_by wall-clock time [for inference and source reliability estimation] Computational efficiency is evaluated through wall-clock measurements for inference and source reliability estimation. The experiments use the NQ dataset, a Beta prior, and a single RTX 6000 Ada GPU.

s: The inference phase, measured by wall-clock time, evaluates Vanilla RAG, Self-RAG, and the method across source counts; the method rises from 1.21 seconds at 5 sources to 1.82 seconds at 1,000, with parallelizable tasks and filtering per source.

l: Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: This study evaluates 13 open-source large language models for question answering in Quranic studies using a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Rather than using the Qur’an text itself, the system retrieves semantically relevant descriptive material on Quranic surahs, including their meanings, historical context, and qualities; the records describe the dataset as covering the 114 surahs, with one account specifying descriptive information for 20 surahs. Models generate cited responses grounded in this retrieved context. Human evaluators score Context Relevance, Answer Faithfulness, and Answer Relevance on five-point Likert scales, while Fleiss’ Kappa measures evaluator agreement, ranging from 0.80 to 0.93. The work aims to improve reliable, transparent, contextually faithful responses and reduce hallucinations in a religiously and culturally sensitive domain. Across Llama, Gemma, QwQ, and Phi models, larger models generally perform best, with Llama3:70b, Llama3.1:70b, and Gemma2:27b identified as leading performers but computationally demanding. Gemma2:9b and Llama3:8b offer efficiency-performance trade-offs. Small models usually score lower, yet Llama3.2:3b stands out with strong faithfulness and answer relevance, performing comparably to larger models in some respects. The study concludes that RAG improves answer quality through external domain-specific grounding, while practical model choice depends on accuracy, speed, and available computational resources.

l: large language models, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Large language models are general-purpose models that handle activities including summarization, translation, domain-specific question answering, annotation, and response generation from retrieved descriptions. In the study, 13 open-source models are used for Quranic-studies queries in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, operating zero-shot without fine-tuning on the dataset. Because Quranic studies are sensitive and domain-specific, the central concerns are accuracy, contextual relevance, authenticity, distortion, and hallucination. The models are assessed through human evaluation of Context Relevance, Answer Faithfulness, and Answer Relevance, and grouped by parameter size as small, medium, or large. Performance varies by size: larger models generally provide higher-quality, more accurate and contextually faithful responses and are suited to high-accuracy tasks, but they impose greater computational demands. The study therefore compares response quality, faithfulness, performance, and efficiency while highlighting the trade-off between model scale and computational resources.

l: Qur’anic studies, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Quranic studies is a sensitive, domain-specific field and task for NLP, large language models, question answering, and knowledge retrieval. It concerns queries about the meanings, historical context, qualities, and descriptive material of Quranic surahs. The work emphasizes accurate, contextually relevant, trustworthy responses, with Islamic scholarship and expert review used to ensure authenticity and exclude speculation. It supplies the questions and queries used to evaluate a RAG system and 13 LLMs.

l: hallucinations, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Hallucinations are a major problem in generated language-model responses: they deviate from authoritative sources and may be factually inaccurate, irrelevant, or unsubstantiated. They especially threaten reliability in religious and culturally sensitive contexts. Retrieval-Augmented Generation, retrieved external knowledge, and source citations are used to reduce them by grounding responses.

l: domain-specific knowledge, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: is_integrated_by Retrieval-Augmented Generation [to maintain response quality] Domain-specific knowledge is integrated to improve response accuracy, relevance, and faithfulness. The study supplies this knowledge through a dataset about Quranic surahs.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a method that addresses problems associated with using separate models by gathering relevant knowledge before generating a response. It combines semantic retrieval with large language model generation, integrating large language model semantics and a vector database to search vectorized descriptive datasets. Relevant entries are supplied to models, enabling contextually relevant, dataset-based answers grounded in authoritative, contextually appropriate, external domain-specific knowledge and accompanied by citations for traceability and transparency. Its central effects are improved response quality and relevance, reduced hallucinations, and more reliable outputs. In the evaluated models, large models benefit most, while medium and small models improve but remain limited in integrating retrieved knowledge. It is also applied in the medical domain to mitigate retrieval and generation issues.

l: large models, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Large language models include Llama3:70b, Gemma2:27b, and QwQ:32b. They outperform medium and small models by capturing query semantics, producing accurate and contextually grounded responses, and showing stronger context understanding, faithfulness, and relevance. Their larger parameter sizes improve context relevance and reduce hallucination, and they benefit most from Retrieval-Augmented Generation. However, substantial memory and processing needs limit use in resource-constrained environments.

l: medium models, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Medium models are large language models including Gemma2:9b, Llama3:8b, and Llama3.1:8b. They strongly deliver answer faithfulness and relevance relative to size, balancing efficiency and response quality for moderately complex tasks, though with lower context relevance than large models.

l: small models, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Small models are large language models including Llama3.2:3b and Phi3:3.8b. They are computationally efficient for lightweight, domain-specific tasks but generally score lower and struggle with complex queries requiring sophisticated semantic understanding. Well-optimized smaller architectures show promise, with Llama3.2:3b achieving stronger results.

l: Llama3:70b, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Llama3:70b, a large models entity, achieves 4.571 in answer faithfulness and relevance with Kappa 0.92, consistently delivering superior performance while computational demands challenge practical deployment.

l: Gemma2:27b, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Gemma2:27b is a large models entity that delivers superior context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance, scoring 0.429, 4.238, and 4.381 with Kappa 0.90, though computational demands challenge deployment.

l: Gemma2:9b, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Gemma2:9b, a medium model, leads medium models in context relevance at 0.492, with 4.143 answer faithfulness and relevance and 0.92 Kappa; it balances efficiency and performance and suits moderately complex tasks.

l: Llama3:8b, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Llama3:8b, a medium model, balances efficiency and performance, suits moderately complex tasks, and achieves varied relevance and faithfulness scores.

l: Llama3.2:3b, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Llama3.2:3b is a small LLM and small model evaluated for context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance. It begins as a small-model entry but emerges as an outlier in the experimental results: it scores 0.508 on context relevance, 4.619 on answer faithfulness, and 4.857 on answer relevance, with a Kappa value of 0.90. Its faithfulness and relevance scores are the highest reported and outperform medium models and a number of large models. In these aspects it performs comparably to larger models, suggesting that architectural improvements, pre-training quality, data efficiency, and architectural optimizations can partly offset smaller parameter size.

l: 114 surahs of the Qur’an, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: The Qur’an comprises 114 surahs, described by names, objectives, revelation contexts, virtues, relationships, meanings, historical context, and qualities; in reading order, it unfolds as individual surahs whose descriptive information supports contextually faithful answers.

l: descriptive dataset of Quranic surahs, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: This is a structured descriptive dataset about the 114 surahs of the Qur’an, derived from a book about those surahs rather than from the Qur’an text itself. It records each surah’s number of verses, name meaning and reason, general objective, provenance or reason for revelation when available, historical context, virtues, and relationships between surahs and their parts. It therefore supplies contextual and interpretative details beyond the actual text. A preliminary study selected 20 surahs. The material was digitized, structured, validated, vectorized into text embeddings with NLP models, and stored in a vector database for efficient retrieval. Its central role is to provide curated external domain-specific knowledge for a Retrieval-Augmented Generation architecture: models retrieve pertinent information before responding, supporting descriptive Quranic-studies tasks, evaluation of responses, contextual correctness, and credible, relevant answers.

l: Context Relevance, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Context relevance is an evaluation metric and one of three criteria used by human evaluators to assess model performance. It measures how precisely retrieved information and generated responses align with a user query and its context while avoiding irrelevant content. It is illustrated by Precision@k for top-k retrieved results and scored from 1 to 5. Large models generally score higher, though Llama3.2:3b reaches 0.508 and exceeds several medium and large models.

l: Answer Faithfulness, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models
s: Answer faithfulness is a human-evaluated evaluation metric for assessing whether generated responses accurately reflect retrieved information and datasets, without unsupported claims, inaccuracies, or hallucinations. Evaluators compare responses with retrieved content and score factual consistency. It is one of three human-evaluated metrics used to assess model performance. Large and medium models generally perform strongly; Llama3.2:3b has the highest reported score, 4.619, and Llama3.2:1b the lowest, 1.381.
